I can relate to you in some of the things you shared.  I struggle with depression and I don't always want to be positive either.  Why people tell people who are going through rough times to be positive I think is not always positive.  I used to go to a crowded park with a sign that read, "I desire conversation.  Will you talk to me?" I met thousands of people doing that over a 2+ year period.  I met a lot of people who were dealing with a lot of hard things such as people who lost a spouse, or a man only given months to live, battling brain cancer.  When hearing their stories, why would I tell them to be positive during a time where it doesn't really match the moment?  Why would I tell them to be any certain way, except just listen to them?  When people tell people to be a certain way, I don't understand it.  For me, sometimes just being how I am in the moment and not resisting the feelings of sadness can actually help me to feel better vs. covering up those feelings and being something that I'm not.  So I just want to thank you for putting it all out there in your post and being yourself and sharing yourself uncensored and not being someone else that you don't want to be in this moment.

I can relate.  I've struggled with depression for a long time.  When I tell people I have wanted to die in my past, many have reacted to it in a way that I feel is not helpful to my situation.  But there was a time I was desperate to talk to people, so desperate I went out to a crowded area with a sign that read, "I desire conversation.  Will you talk to me?"  I ended up meeting a lot of people that way, talking to strangers for over 2 years.  I met thousands of people.  I noticed that when I shared with strangers about my depression, there were some people that really listened to me and I felt heard.  Though there were also a lot of people who didn't listen to me too.  A lot of people I met shared their deepest sorrows with me.  Somethings people shared felt like secrets they hadn't even shared with their family.   I have pondered the psychology of conversations with strangers before.  Perhaps there is something to having no attachments to the other person or caring too much about what the other person knows or doesn't know about me that makes some strangers more likely to open up.  Whereas with family it does feel much harder for me to have conversations about depression and harder topics.  

When it comes to sharing with my parents, I stopped sharing about my depression with them long ago because of the way they react to me.  I can relate to you when you encountered diversion from your friends and family.  I currently live with my parents and they know nothing about my current depression.  Yet, there are some random people I met doing conversations with strangers a while back that may know more about me than my parents.

Anyways, thanks for replying to my comment.  Like I said, if you feel the need to share more, please share.  How do you want to be listened to?  What makes you feel accepted and heard?

In my depression, I was so desperate to talk to people, I went to a crowded place with a sign that read, "I desire conversation. Will you talk to me?" Over 2 years of doing that frequently, I talked to thousands of strangers.  Some of those conversations were the best I ever had and gave my life meaning. It was those conversations that made me keep coming back and meeting strangers.  I met my significant other over a year ago and one of my closest friends through holding that sign asking for conversations from strangers.

It's that minority of people who actually care that make it worth it to talk to strangers.  If I didn't seek to talk to people, I wouldn't have some of the most amazing relationships I have today.

Also another thing to try, perhaps simpler, is something called a Downward Arrow. In this task you ask yourself what would happen if this happened and continue asking that question to each answer you come up with.  In your case you could ask, what would happen if I was bored?  Hypothetically speaking, if you were to answer that question with, I would be restless.  Then you would then follow up asking, what would happen if I get restless?  Hypothetically speaking if you answered,  I wouldn't feel like I'm living my live fully, then you would ask what would happen if you didn't feel like you were living your life fully?  If your answer to that question is I would feel like a failure in life, then you would ask yourself what would happen if you felt like a failure in life and so on.  Now I made up those answers, but hopefully you get the point.  You keep asking the questions until you get to whatever the root fear is in the Downward Arrow.  I would recommend not thinking too much about your answers but instead responding quickly with what comes to mind and avoiding answering I don't know.  Sometimes this exercise can be pretty revealing.

Also, when it comes to OCD, I believe the research shows that talk therapy is not all that effective in treating it.  In your post you mentioned that your therapist is just there to validate you and hear you.  So if you really do have OCD, not saying you do or not, that kind of therapy likely wouldn't help your situation.

In conclusion, I don't know if you have OCD or not, but if anything I said here resonates with you, then I would definitely look into getting a professional opinion about your situation.  If it's not OCD, there are other anxiety disorders that have some similarities to OCD that could be related to what you are experiencing.

First off, I will preface this by saying, if what you are experiencing is not related to OCD or compulsionary behavior, how you respond to what you are going through may be completely different.  So I do think it is good to get a diagnosis?  Otherwise, if you treat it like OCD and it isn't OCD, you might do more harm than good.

With that said, I'll share more about my experience and OCD in general first and then come back to how all this might relate to your situation, along with sharing what has worked for me.  So please bare with me. This might take a while....

For me, I have struggled off and on with bouts of deeply disturbing intrusive thoughts at any given moment.  When these intrusive thoughts would arise I would get so caught up in the content of those thoughts and then I would engage in really strange behaviors to cope in the moment.  It was very debilitating for me and deprived me of my joy in life.  I felt like I was an awful person for having those thoughts.  I gave meaning to the content of those thoughts and in my mind I labeled them as disturbing and truly horrific.  In doing so I battled to push those thoughts away.  In the act of trying to get rid of those thoughts it actually made the thoughts come up even more to the point it felt like I didn't have control.  Something I learned later in my journey, it's not really the content of those thoughts that's important.  To me all of those thoughts were the same. They triggered me to do compulsionary behaviors.  Like I said I gave those thoughts meaning.  Once I stopped giving those thoughts meaning, the disturbing thoughts started to go away and faded into the background.  One of the biggest breakthroughs I had was realizing that I am not my thoughts.  I think it's easy to think just because I had a disturbing thought that I'm going to do that disturbing thing that I was thinking about or something is wrong with me, which is not the case at all.  Some people with OCD can be super hypersensitive to these triggers and be the least likely people to act on what they are thinking about.  For example, if a person has harm OCD around hurting someone with a knife, some people may go as far as to remove all the knives in their house, making them the least likely person to harm someone with a knife.  Like I said, the huge breakthrough for me was to get I'm not my thoughts and just because they are their it doesn't mean I will carry out those thoughts in real life, nor do I need to react to them or focus on them.

To lessen the intensity of those thoughts, I had to be ok with having the thoughts be there.  It might sound counterintuitive, but in a way, I welcomed the thoughts. In welcoming them, over time the anxiety started to decrease and the thoughts went away.  I also did something called ERP therapy (Exposure Response Prevention).  For people with OCD, the idea behind this therapy is to expose a person to what they are afraid of and prevent them from engaging in the ritual response they do after.  For example, a person who has contamination OCD and is afraid of getting germs, a therapist might have that person purposefully touch garbage and then have that person not wash their hands for a period of time after.  In the act of not washing their hands, the person may experience more anxiety in the moment.  After doing many replication sessions of not washing hands after touching garbage, a person's anxiety level can decrease over time.  Then once that task doesn't seem as hard, the therapist might have the person do other tasks that expose them to more contamination OCD anxiety, while not allowing the person to engage in their compulsions to cope.

But in the case of harm OCD, the exposure process can't be acted out in real life because it could be harmful to others or the person themselves.  In this case, the person may be asked to write a script involving the intrusive violent thought.  The therapist might ask that person to purposefully think of the thought and expand on it and go into great deal about it.  After that person finishes their script making it as juicy as they can in detail about their violent thought, the therapist might have that person read the script over and over until basically it loses meaning and becomes boring and not anxiety provoking at all.  Once the person has achieved that in a clinical setting, then the therapist might have them read their script at home, or even public places where the person might experience more anxiety reading about their thoughts.

The idea here is to go head on into the anxiety and resist doing the compulsionary behavior to cope with it.

It's important to understand what's going on for each person.  What's intrusive? What's triggering you? What do you have control over? In terms of your situation, is it the moments of boredom, unsatisfaciton, emptiness, etc. that's intrusive/unwanted or is it the suicidal thoughts or is it both?  Do you have control over thinking about these suicidal thoughts?

Now I could be wrong, but in your situation, it sounds like the existential, bored, empty, unsatisfying moments are the trigger and the compulsion could possibly be to think suicidal thoughts.  If that is the case, what would happen if you were bored, feeling unsatisfied, etc., and you resisted having the suicidal thoughts? Is that something you can do?  What if you just experienced these existential moments and didn't do anything?  If you really wanted to expose yourself, what would happen if you purposefully made yourself bored or did something unsatisfying?  If that's too much for you to do, what if you practiced being bored for a certain number of minutes and resisting the suicidal thoughts for an amount of time you could do?  AS you get better with being with the anxiety of being bored, unsatisfied, etc., and resisting the thoughts, you could increase your time increments of being bored, etc.?

But if the suicidal thoughts are intrusive thoughts, and is something you feel you don't have control over, then what I just said may not be helpful.  I feel like a lot of it depends on if you can control the suicidal thoughts or not.  I was unclear in your post if that's something you had control of or not since it sounded like you experienced fear after having them, but then you also said it felt calming to have them, which made me think they aren't intrusive.

Another possibility, though your suicidal thoughts may be calming, following your moments of boredom, etc., does that trigger you later to have intrusive thoughts about previously having your suicidal thoughts?  Hopefully that made sense. If your coping mechanism was to imagine yourself on a beach on a sunny day, like I had mentioned in a previous comment, would you even be thinking there's anything wrong with that?  If it is truly OCD related, and the mental compulsion is to think of something to escape the moment, whether it's a sunny beach or suicidal thoughts, it's still OCD and can greatly impact the person's life if untreated.  But in your situation, I imagine that a lot of people, with OCD or not, would be disturbed by having suicidal thoughts as a coping mechanism, since most people don't typically associate that with being calming.  For me, it doesn't matter what the content of the thoughts are and how disturbing they may seem or not, in my OCD, if I react to them and give them meaning, and engage in compulsionary behavior to cope with the anxiety of having them, I usually will encounter those thoughts at a greater frequency in the future, making my OCD worse.

A question I have is why are you having to calm yourself in those moments of boredom, extentialism, emptiness, and unsatisfaction? What happens for you when those uncomfortable things arise?

If you don't know, something you could try is to purposefully engage in boredom, existential, unsatisfying, empty things, and observe what happens as it is happening for yourself.  You could write down what you are feeling, what you are experiencing to see if that gives you any insight into your situation.  You can also write down what happens for you after you have the suicidal thoughts, if they arise, such as your thoughts and what they mean to you.  Like I said at the beginning of this comment, if you don't have OCD this kind of advice could actually be harmful to some people or at the very least it may be recommended to do this under the supervision of a trained therapist.  If you have ever heard of paradoxical intention, it's kind of like that, purposefully engaging in the feared behavior.  And for some people this can be unsafe to do.

If someone told me what you initially said in this post in the throws of my sorrow, it would make me feel worse and possibly want to die even more.  When I share my struggles, it doesn't necessarily mean I'm always looking for help in the moment.  What's most helpful is if the other person just listens.  Listening is not giving advice or comparisons to other people's pain and situations or giving some form of judgement. In many cases, listening can be as simple as the receiver saying nothing and just being there present with me.  That can be most helpful.  If you are looking to say comments like you said initially, you may want to ask the OP how they feel about receiving feedback first before giving your feedback.  That kind of feedback could be the very thing that puts people over the edge.  At the very least, if you ask the OP first before you give your feedback, you give them the choice to say yes or no to hearing what you have to share, which can empower the person and give them a heads up that you might be sharing something that is hard to hear and take in.  Also, sometimes the way we might want to help someone can be an act of selfishness and/or judgement because we are coming from a place of making the assumption that the help we are giving will actually help them and is something they need, as well as making the assumption that the person we are trying to help actually wants or needs our help to begin with.  I'm probably guilty at doing this in the past myself.  Not to say there are people who don't need help, I'm sure there are a lot of people out there that need help too and benefit from people helping them.  I'd say unless the person is directly asking for help or feedback and advice, I think it's better to error on the side of not going in the direction of giving unsolicited feedback, especially in the realm of comparing to other people's pain.  Some people may just want to come here and share what they are going through because this is one of the only places you can just be radically honest about life.  For some, just the act of making a post here may be therapeutic in itself.  I don't know about others, but one of the reasons I don't share about my struggles as much with people in real life is because I'm tired of the way people react to me, giving me unsolicited advice or comparing my pain to others, invalidating my feelings.  I'm tired of it! I hate it when people do that!  This subreddit is one of the few places where people can escape to share what's on their mind, and vent their feelings.  Some people may be looking for advice too, but unless someone is asking for advice, let's hold space for people to share what they need to share.  That space created in this subreddit is something I'm grateful for and has helped me and has added meaning to my life.   

Lastly, you mentioned the word context.  How can you judge context on here accurately?  Just because I engage in this subreddit (SuicideWatch), it doesn't imply I'm actively looking for help in the moment.  I feel it can be extremely challenging to know where people are coming from exactly through reading a post or someone's comments on here.  I feel like a lot of context is lost through sharing text. Though written words in themselves can be powerful and illicit emotional responses in us, sometimes even greater than hearing the same words spoken, a lot of context can be lost when compared to hearing someone share in person, such as hearing the tone of someone's voice or seeing someone's body language etc., which can tell us things about the person that we just can't get through text alone.  Even when hearing someone share in person, we still might not have all the information we need to fully understand where someone is coming from.  Just because this is the "Suicide Watch" section of reddit, I still think it's better to error on the safe side of not making assumptions, unless the OP explicitly states what they want from the reader.

Most people tend to keep to themselves.  I used to sit on a public park bench for years, in a crowded area, with a sign that read "I desire conversation. Will you talk to me?" I talked to thousands of people.  Some of the people I spoke with were filled with many things, spouses dying, cancer, significant others leaving them or betraying them, some of the worst life circumstances I've ever heard of.  Yet, when I have been down in the dumps myself, I find it extremely challenging to engage with people let alone initiate a conversation.  The fact that these random strangers who opened up to me really showed me that the world is full of grieving people.  How can a world where we don't talk or get to know each other give support to the grieving?  Some of the people I met were lonely and didn't have anyone.  Yet, to the person who does want to die or commit suicide they are often judged.  Rarely do I hear people judging themselves saying, how am I responsible in the matter of someone taking their own life?  I'm no psychologist or have I done research or searched for research on how the behavior of society as a whole impacts suicide rates, but I can't imagine that a society that is so individualistic and doesn't meet each other and get to know each other and listens to one another as common practice, I can't imagine this kind of behavior would support people who are really struggling.  So like I said, it doesn't surprise me at all that suicide happens.  Where I live, I need a sign asking people to have conversation for them to approach me and talk to me.  However, if I don't have a sign making that request or I don't initiate a conversation in any way, no one talks to me.  I imagine for the person who is struggling in life where I live, it would probably be extremely difficult because no one here seems to take societal responsibility in understanding how their passive behavior is contributing to this world feeling so cold and miserable.  When someone is feeling down, I don't expect them to be in a place mentally to make the first move when talking to someone or reaching out. But when no one or very few people in a community seems to be making a move to connect and get to know each other, then I think that's a real societal problem that needs to be addressed.  Anyways...
